title: Runtime type guard at the collab frame decode boundary
wave: Wave 1 — Lifecycle foundation (W1, W2, W3, W5). First in sequence, no gate in front of it.
one_line: Replace the blind `as CollabFrame` cast at the end of `open()` with a per-variant required-field check, so a structurally broken frame is rejected at the network boundary instead of surfacing as a meaningless TypeError several calls later.
user_visible_effect: none — internal. A malformed or tampered collab frame is now dropped at the decrypt boundary with a named reason in the debug log, instead of being handed to the host/guest frame handler as a well-typed lie. Users never see this; it only changes what lands in `~/.omp/logs/omp.<date>.log` on the `collab: ignoring undecryptable guest frame` line.

test_contract: The observable contract: a collab frame whose JSON payload is structurally inconsistent with its own variant is rejected at the decrypt boundary, by an error whose message names the variant and the missing field — not handed to the frame handler as a value typed `CollabFrame` but lacking a field every consumer of that variant will read. A consumer of this contract observes three things. (1) Every one of the 18 declared `CollabFrame` variants survives a `seal`/`open` round trip byte-for-byte, so the guard can never become a forward-compatibility regression. (2) A payload missing a required field, or whose `t` is absent / not a string, rejects at `open()` — today those resolve successfully and blow up later as an unrelated TypeError inside `CollabHost`/`CollabGuestLink`. (3) A payload carrying a variant tag this build has never seen still opens successfully, so an older or newer peer is not rejected. If the guard regresses to an exact-shape check, test 1 goes red; if the tolerant default is dropped, test 4 goes red; if the guard is deleted, tests 2 and 3 go red.

blocks: W8 (Wave 3a) — the plan asks for all collab boundary work to land in one review pass
Any later work that adds a `CollabFrame` variant: the `Record<CollabFrame["t"], …>` annotation turns a forgotten guard row into a compile error, which is a deliberate coupling
effort: S. ~50 lines added to crypto.ts (a 48-line map plus a 20-line function, on a 67-line file) and ~75 lines added to the existing test file. The production change itself is a one-line edit at crypto.ts:57; the fixture table is the bulk. Verified end to end on a scratch branch: applied, type-checked, tested, then reverted — the repo is clean.
risk: A false-positive rejection is far more expensive than the defect it fixes. `open()` has exactly one production caller — `packages/coding-agent/src/collab/relay-client.ts:578` — and its catch block routes by role: on the host it logs and drops the frame (line 582), but on the GUEST it calls `#failFatal("bad key or corrupted frame")` (line 584), which sets `#closed = true`, closes the socket, and fires `onClose(reason, false)` with no reconnect (relay-client.ts:675-689). So a guard that is one field too strict does not drop a frame — it tears the guest's collab session down permanently and tells the user to rejoin. The plan's stated rationale ("a throw only loses one frame, because #recvChain has a .catch() at the tail") is wrong on both counts: the tail `.catch()` at relay-client.ts:595-597 covers errors from `onFrame?.()`, and `open()` is already wrapped in its own try/catch at 577-586. This inverts the priority — permissiveness is the requirement, strictness is the cost. The single field most likely to bite is `data` on the `bus` variant, typed `unknown`: if any future `emitSubagentFrame(channel, payload)` call site ever passes `undefined`, `JSON.stringify` drops the key and every guest connected to that host dies. Today this is unreachable — all 6 emit sites (packages/coding-agent/src/task/executor.ts:1497, 1597, 2641, 2947, 3321, 4065) pass concrete object literals. If it ever becomes reachable, drop `"data"` from the `bus` row rather than tightening anything else.
open_questions: Should the `data` field on the `bus` variant stay in the required list? Keeping it matches the `CollabFrame` type and passes the 'missing required field' test faithfully; dropping it is strictly safer against a future `undefined` emit and costs nothing observable. Default to keeping it (the current type says required and no call site violates it), and revisit only if a new `emitSubagentFrame` call site can pass `undefined`.

Should the guard be exported for reuse? No. `sealSerialized` is already exported and lets the tests build malformed payloads without one, and keeping the guard module-private means the test can only observe it through `open()` — which is the contract the item is actually about. Exporting would add a surface with no consumer.

Does the guard belong at the `JSON.parse` boundary in crypto.ts, or one layer up in relay-client? crypto.ts. The plan's call is right: crypto.ts is the only module that knows both the ciphertext framing and the `CollabFrame` type, and it is the single place every decoded frame passes through (`git grep -n 'as CollabFrame' -- packages/` finds no other production site).

plan_corrections.claim: "#recvChain có .catch() ở đuôi nên một lần ném chỉ mất một frame" — a throw from the guard costs at most one frame.
plan_corrections.correction: The tail `.catch()` does not cover the guard at all. `open()` is called inside its own try/catch (relay-client.ts:577-586); the chain's `.catch()` at 595-597 only catches errors thrown by `onFrame?.()` on line 594. The inner catch routes by role: host → `logger.debug` and drop (line 582); GUEST → `#failFatal("bad key or corrupted frame")` (line 584), and `#failFatal` sets `#closed = true`, closes the socket, discards pending sends and calls `onClose(reason, false)` with reconnect disabled. A false-positive guard rejection therefore kills the guest's session outright. The plan's threat framing is still right that this is defense-in-depth rather than a security fix (the guard sits behind AES-256-GCM and the relay is a content-blind byte pump), but the 'cheap to be wrong about' conclusion does not hold, and the design must stay maximally permissive.

plan_corrections.claim: The guard is a per-variant required-field check covering all frame variants crossing the decode boundary.
plan_corrections.correction: The plan does not say how many variants there are. There are exactly 18 discriminants: abort, agent-cmd, agents, bus, bye, entry, error, event, fetch-transcript, hello, prompt, snapshot-chunk, state, transcript, ui-request, ui-request-end, ui-response, welcome. Annotating the map as `Record<CollabFrame["t"], readonly string[]>` (rather than a plain `Record<string, …>`) makes a forgotten variant a compile error — verified: deleting the `error` row produces TS2741 naming all 18 literals. That is strictly better than the plan's hand-maintained list and should be used.
